# Lite requirements document — Pull request checklist

A written pull request checklist for this repository: a `CONTRIBUTING.md` at the root that
states the five things every pull request must include, and one README sentence pointing
to it. It matters because two to five outside contributors, the first users of the
ai-delivery kit (the Claude Code skills this repository exercises), arrive by 2026-10-05.
Today they would learn the standard only at review, after their work is done.

## 1. Problem & Context

**What problem does this solve?**
Nobody opening a pull request here has a written standard for what it must include. The
conventions for branch names, commit scope, running the tests, descriptions and issue
links exist only in the maintainer's head, drawn from a year of the maintainer's own
review comments. Outside contributors would meet them only at review, after the branch is
named, the commits are shaped and the description is written, so every miss means
redoing finished work.

**Who is affected?**
- **Outside contributors (two to five people):** the kit's first users. They know the kit
  from its README but have never worked in this repository. Without the standard, their
  first pull requests come back for rework. They are likely to open pull requests through
  the kit itself; that is an assumption, tested by open question 1.
- **The maintainer, Max Adamsky:** today the only author and reviewer. Without the
  standard, the maintainer answers the same questions one contributor at a time. The
  maintainer keeps the count behind the success measure below and signs off on this
  document.

**What exists today?**
- No written contribution guidance: no `CONTRIBUTING.md`, no pull request template and no
  license. The kit's conventions record, `.ai-delivery/conventions.md`, is written for the
  kit's skills and has no rule for any of the five items.
- Branches in use are the agent-made `codex/<topic>-<number>` branches, plus
  `live-proof-2026-09-21`.
- Three draft pull requests (#1 to #3) are open, all produced by the kit's ship skill,
  which is its commit-and-pull-request workflow. None of them targets `main`, and no pull
  request has ever merged. `main` has not changed since 2026-08-28.
- GitHub issues are enabled on the repository, but none has ever been filed.
- The repository has no Python modules and no tests. `uv run pytest` exits with code 5,
  meaning no tests were collected (checked 2026-09-22).

**How success is judged:**
- **Threshold.** Across the first ten pull requests from outside contributors, count those
  that needed a comment asking for one of the four items a reviewer can see from the pull
  request: item 1 (branch name), item 2 (commit scope), item 4 (a description that says
  why) and item 5 (a linked issue). One or none means it worked. Exactly two is
  inconclusive. Three or more means it did not work. Item 3 stays out of the count until
  tests exist, because a reviewer cannot see whether it was done.
- **Count.** From the first outside pull request onward, the maintainer records which
  items needed a comment. How the count is run is open question 7.
- **Timing.** The checklist is in place, and linked from the README, before the first
  outside contributor opens a pull request.

---

## 2. Scope

**In Scope:**
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` at the repository root: about 30 lines, holding five items. Each item
  is one imperative sentence plus one example.
- One sentence at the end of `README.md` pointing to it, together with the refreshed kit
  setup record that editing `README.md` requires. **[ASSUMPTION — open question 4]**

**Out of Scope:**
- Automated enforcement of any kind, including CI checks and hooks.
- A pull request template.
- A code of conduct.
- A release process.
- Anything about how the kit itself works, including how to use or override its ship
  skill. Open question 1 asks whether that line should move.
- A "Contributing" section inside `README.md`. The README gets one sentence, not a
  section.
- A license file. It was not requested. Whether one is needed before the first outside
  contribution is open question 10.
- Protecting `main` with branch rules. That is enforcement under the rule above, and open
  question 9 asks whether it is needed first.
- Rewriting item 3 once tests exist. What triggers that is open question 8.
- Adopting a published contributing-guide skeleton. The CC0-licensed
  `nayafia/contributing-template` was consulted as a wording reference only. It covers
  none of the five items specifically.
- Any change to the kit.

---

## 3. Units of Work

- **Unit 1 (Urgent): Publish the pull request checklist in CONTRIBUTING.md.** An outside
  contributor can read the five things every pull request here must include before naming
  a branch or writing a commit. The checklist is reachable from the repository page's
  Contributing tab and sidebar link, and from the links GitHub adds to its new-issue and
  new-pull-request pages. This unit touches only `CONTRIBUTING.md`, a new file.
- **Unit 2 (High): Link the pull request checklist from the README.** A contributor who
  starts from the README, the first thing the kit's users read, reaches the checklist in
  one step. This unit touches only `README.md` and the kit's setup record. Its link target
  is fixed as `CONTRIBUTING.md` at the repository root, so both units can be built at the
  same time.

**Happy path:** Contributor opens the repository → follows the Contributing link or the
README sentence → reads the five items → names the branch, shapes the commits and runs the
tests as the items say → opens a pull request with a paragraph saying why and a linked
GitHub issue → review asks for none of the five → Done

---

## 4. Requirements

| ID | Description | Priority | Acceptance Criteria |
|----|-------------|----------|---------------------|
| FR-001 | `CONTRIBUTING.md` at the repository root holds the pull request checklist. | Urgent | The file exists at the root. It has a title, at most one introductory sentence, and exactly five numbered items in the order FR-002 to FR-006, each one imperative sentence followed by one example. It runs to about 30 lines. It covers none of the out-of-scope topics and does not describe how the kit works. Once the file is on `main`, GitHub shows it as the repository's Contributing tab and sidebar link, and links it from the new-issue and new-pull-request pages. |
| FR-002 | Item 1 says how to name a branch. | Urgent | The item says to name the branch `<GitHub handle>/<short topic>` and gives one example, such as `octocat/fix-readme-typo`. It says the `codex/` prefix is reserved for branches made by agents. |
| FR-003 | Item 2 says how to scope commits. | Urgent | The item says to make one commit per change, and gives one example showing what one change means. **[ASSUMPTION — open question 2]** "Per change" means one commit per logical change, so a pull request may hold several commits. |
| FR-004 | Item 3 says to run the tests before opening a pull request. | High | The item says to run `uv run pytest` before opening a pull request. It says that until the first test module lands, "no tests ran" (pytest's exit code 5) is the expected result. Running the command in this repository exits with code 5 (checked 2026-09-22). This is High rather than Urgent because a reviewer cannot see from a pull request whether it was done, so it stays out of the success count until tests exist. |
| FR-005 | Item 4 asks for a description that says why. | Urgent | The item asks for a one-paragraph pull request description saying why the change was made, and gives a one-paragraph example. |
| FR-006 | Item 5 asks for a linked GitHub issue. | Urgent | The item asks for a link to a GitHub issue on this repository in the pull request description, and gives one example of the link. It says the maintainer adds any Linear link at review. GitHub issues are enabled on this repository (checked 2026-09-22). **[ASSUMPTION — open question 5]** The contributor files the issue, or picks an existing one, before starting work. |
| FR-007 | `README.md` points to the checklist. | High | `README.md` ends with one sentence containing a relative link to `CONTRIBUTING.md`, and the link opens the file on GitHub. No other line of `README.md` changes. Once the change lands, the kit's setup check still passes; it reports FRESH, not STALE. **[ASSUMPTION — open question 4]** The refreshed setup record, `.ai-delivery/stack-fingerprint`, lands in the same pull request as the sentence. That file stores a hash of `README.md`. |

**Design-system components:** none. The work is not UI-facing.

**Key constraints:**
- **Deadline.** The checklist must be in place, and linked from the README, before the
  first outside pull request. Contributors arrive by 2026-10-05, two weeks after 2026-09-21,
  a date fixed by the kit's release. **[ASSUMPTION — open question 3]** "In place" means on
  `main` on GitHub, because GitHub reads the Contributing tab from the default branch.
- **`main` lacks the toolchain.** Item 3's command works only where `pyproject.toml` and
  `uv.lock` exist. `main` holds only `.ai-delivery/`, `docs/`, `.gitignore` and a two-line
  README, so item 3 is wrong on `main` until those two files reach it.
- **The setup record.** Editing `README.md` makes the kit's setup check report STALE, and
  every kit skill that checks setup then stops until setup re-runs. Adding
  `CONTRIBUTING.md` does not have this effect (checked against
  `.ai-delivery/stack-fingerprint`, 2026-09-22).
- **Sequencing.** Discovery decided that the README sentence lands ahead of the README
  rewrite queued as Linear issues MAX-16 to MAX-18, which rebase onto it. That rewrite is
  already built (MAX-16 is commit 890dea8, in draft pull request #3), and this branch
  already carries it. So the ordering can hold only on `main`; see open question 4.
- **Tooling and effort.** No new tooling beyond uv and pytest, and no automated
  enforcement. The work takes a few hours at most. The repository is the kit's test bed,
  so changes stay small and ordinary.

## Open Questions

Every question below is open, and Max Adamsky owns each one. The brief's section 10 rates
the risks behind questions 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8.

- [ ] **1. Does a pull request exactly as the kit's ship skill produces it meet the
  standard?** Ship suggests a `feat/…` branch, writes a multi-section description and
  links Linear rather than a GitHub issue. If it does not meet the standard, may the guide
  say how to override ship, given that anything about how the kit works is excluded?
  Otherwise contributors must choose between the guide and the kit, and the count
  measures that conflict instead of the guide. *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before the
  guide is written (affects FR-002, FR-005 and FR-006).
- [ ] **2. What does "one commit per change" mean: one squashed commit per pull request,
  or one commit per logical change?** Contributors and ship read it differently, since
  ship commits one unit at a time, and the count includes it. FR-003 assumes one commit
  per logical change. *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before the guide is written.
- [ ] **3. How does `main` receive the checklist, and does "in place" mean on `main` on
  GitHub?**
  - `main` has not changed since 2026-08-28, and no pull request has ever merged into it.
  - This branch is 20 commits ahead of `main` and has not been pushed.
  - `main` has no `pyproject.toml` or `uv.lock`.

  *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before 2026-10-05.
- [ ] **4. How do the README sentence and the refreshed setup record land together, and
  how does the sentence relate to MAX-16's rewrite?** The rewrite is already built (commit
  890dea8, draft pull request #3), and this branch already carries it. FR-007 assumes one
  pull request carries both the sentence and the refreshed record. *Owner:* Max Adamsky.
  *Needed:* before unit 2 is built.
- [ ] **5. Who files the GitHub issue a contributor links, and when? Who triages GitHub
  issues?** No GitHub issue has ever been filed here, and item 5 would leave the
  maintainer running a second tracker. FR-006 assumes the contributor files or picks the
  issue before starting work. *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before the guide is
  written.
- [ ] **6. May contributor pull requests change `.ai-delivery/` and `docs/decisions.md`?
  Would saying so in the guide count as describing the kit?** Running kit setup rewrites
  those shared files. That puts unrelated changes into pull requests and makes
  contributors working in parallel conflict. *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before
  2026-10-05.
- [ ] **7. How is the count run?** Four things are undecided:
  - Is each contributor's first pull request reported separately?
  - Does a miss the contributor fixed without being asked count?
  - Where is the count kept?
  - By what date is the verdict read?

  Without these, the threshold can pass or fail for reasons unrelated to the guide.
  *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before the first outside pull request.
- [ ] **8. What triggers the rewrite of item 3 once the first test module lands, and how
  does a contributor tell "no tests yet" from "tests not collected"?** Exit code 5 will
  later mean tests silently failed to be collected. *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* by
  the time the first test module lands.
- [ ] **9. Will contributors push branches to this repository or work from forks? Does
  `main` need protection before they arrive?** The handle prefix matters only for
  branches pushed here. Anyone with write access can push straight to an unprotected
  `main` and skip all five items. Protection is a GitHub setting, and this phase's
  no-enforcement rule currently excludes it. *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before
  2026-10-05.
- [ ] **10. Does the repository need a license before the first outside contribution?**
  The repository is public with no license, so the terms that cover a contribution are
  unanswered. *Owner:* Max Adamsky. *Needed:* before the first outside pull request.

**Next action:** Max Adamsky settles open questions 1, 2 and 5 before the guide is
written, and the rest by the dates above.
